reviewScope.question: Evaluate separately: (1) published firsthand accounts of a 2004 visual encounter; (2) independent radar-operator reports and raw-sensor access; (3) the provenance of the later official infrared video and its connection to the encounter; (4) quantitative speed/acceleration claims; and (5) object origin. Avoid a single blanket 0–100 case or personal believability score.
reviewScope.claim: David Fravor publicly described a firsthand 2004 naval aviation encounter with a white elongated object that appeared to manoeuvre unusually.

distinctAssertions.assertion: Fravor gave this account in official 2023 House testimony.
distinctAssertions.finding: Documented by official record; this alone confirms attribution, not the occurrence or physical properties of the reported object.

distinctAssertions.assertion: Multiple aircrew observed an unusual object during a November 2004 flight.
distinctAssertions.finding: Fravor and named pilot Alex Dietrich gave distinct firsthand descriptions relating to one shared sortie. The publicly inspected sources do not validate every inferred size, distance or speed.

distinctAssertions.assertion: The object traversed roughly sixty miles in less than a minute.
distinctAssertions.finding: Fravor attributed this to an air controller's report to him. The contemporaneous radar tracks and calibrated chronology were not reviewed or accessible here; numerical motion remains unverified.

distinctAssertions.assertion: FLIR1 is a continuous recording of Fravor's original visual sighting.
distinctAssertions.finding: Not supported: Fravor explicitly described a different crew obtaining the infrared video later. The DoD acknowledged a Navy video from November 2004, not that it was recorded by Fravor.

distinctAssertions.assertion: The target had physically exceptional acceleration or a nonhuman origin.
distinctAssertions.finding: Not established by this draft; no verified original time-aligned Princeton/Nimitz/E-2 tracks and sensor-calibrated range or metadata were available for independent kinematic reconstruction.

excludes: No general rating of Fravor's honesty, integrity, reliability or character.
No claim that a score is the probability of any event or alien hypothesis being true.
No extrapolation from other UAP videos or cases to the 2004 Nimitz event.

criteria.title: Original claim recorded accurately and in context
criteria.finding: The official GPO House transcript documents Fravor's attributed 2023 first-person account, including that his aircraft did not get a fire-control radar return and that a later crew filmed the video.
criteria.limits: This is a measure of accurate attribution only; it does not validate the unusual performance.
criteria.nextAudit: Second human editor independently checks full 2023 official transcript, written statement and chronology without accepting the extraordinary interpretation.

criteria.title: Corroboration from demonstrably independent evidence
criteria.finding: At least two separately attributable named pilots, Fravor and Alex Dietrich, report the same flight encounter; additional aircrew and shipboard operators are reported, but must be identified and source-chain audited separately. Radar operator Kevin Day's later account is described in a peer-reviewed analysis, not an available first-generation radar dataset.
criteria.whyNotFull: No independent, time-aligned original sensor reconstruction; same-flight pilots share event context and later coverage reuses that testimony.
criteria.limits: Two independent people describe one shared incident, not a second independent incident. Shared interviews, multiple mentions, and a model constructed from later radar-operator statements cannot each count as a separate instrument trace or proof of measured extreme acceleration.
criteria.nextAudit: Locate separately preserved statements from other aircrew and original mission logs, then evaluate independence and shared recollection/publication lineage.

criteria.title: Accessible original records, measurements and custody
criteria.finding: A DoD-authenticated November 2004 Navy infrared clip is real public instrument evidence recorded on a later sortie. Navy public-affairs records describe the clip's circulation aboard Nimitz. Separately, Fravor attests that Princeton, Nimitz and E-2 systems tracked targets; the original synchronised radar plots are not included in this public review set.
criteria.whyNotFull: The raw first-generation video master, FLIR camera-state metadata, original time-aligned radar tracks, radar calibration, flight logs, and independent same-target linkage between two sorties are not publicly audited here.
criteria.limits: The official release establishes authenticity as Navy footage, not validation of the exact target's physical acceleration or its identity. Reported radar tracking deserves its own source ledger, not a blanket zero because raw logs were not produced publicly. The Navy FOIA briefing is publicly indexed, but its original PDF could not be inspected visually in this pass.
criteria.nextAudit: Request/locate original video master, radar logs, sensor calibration and contemporaneous flight documentation; audit chain of custody and time alignment.

criteria.title: Specific claim scope, methodology and testability
criteria.finding: Reported incident timing, location, relative altitude, object appearance and purported sixty-mile displacement permit falsifiable measurement questions if original sensor inputs become available.
criteria.whyNotFull: Range and motion geometry cannot be reproduced from the statements and later clip alone, without validated metadata and uncertainty bounds.
criteria.limits: A later mathematical model that takes reported ranges/timings as inputs is not a new observation or independent sensor validation.
criteria.nextAudit: Define trajectory ranges, time-source uncertainty, radar calibration, aircraft positions and test multiple mundane/extraordinary models on shared inputs.

criteria.title: Contradictions, alternatives and uncertainty
criteria.finding: Published alternate FLIR1 interpretations include tracking-lock, zoom and camera-motion effects; NASA cautions that sparse data can obstruct identification.
criteria.whyNotFull: Alternatives were identified but not independently reconstructed against original metadata; a FLIR1 explanation need not explain the separate visual observations.
criteria.limits: Mick West's analysis is a competing hypothesis, not an official resolution of the complete Nimitz account; NASA's guidance is general, not a Nimitz-specific verdict.
criteria.nextAudit: Independently test imaging and ordinary-object hypotheses using source imagery, calibrated sensor modes, weather/flight geometry and separate eyewitness claims.

workingTotalInterpretation: No active numeric assessment: the previous combined draft (54/100) was withdrawn after an explicit scope and weighting challenge. The observed-event, reported radar, later official video, extraordinary kinematics and origin propositions require separate reviewed evidence units. Missing raw radar limits precise physics verification; it does not nullify independently attributable pilot testimony or the official video.

sourceRecords.locator: Statement of David Fravor, HTML lines ~830–901; Rep. Langworthy questioning ~2413–2473
sourceRecords.establishes: Fravor's attributable testimony, his own visually described observation, a radar account relayed from ship/controller, and a later video from another crew.
sourceRecords.doesNotEstablish: 2004 radar track data, calibrated acceleration, target identity or nonhuman origin.

sourceRecords.locator: 60 Minutes, 16 May 2021; Fravor and Alex Dietrich direct interview and same-flight narrative
sourceRecords.establishes: Dietrich's own publicly attributed account from the same encounter as Fravor.
sourceRecords.doesNotEstablish: Independent radar measurement, second incident, complete flight record or verified velocity.

sourceRecords.locator: 27 April 2020 release; one video from November 2004, two from January 2015
sourceRecords.establishes: Department's authorization and origin statement about published Navy recordings.
sourceRecords.doesNotEstablish: Raw radar or video master, exact object identity, Fravor's initial visual event filmed, or measured extreme speed.

sourceRecords.locator: 19 December 2019 original Intelligencer Q&A; later sortie ~one hour after Fravor
sourceRecords.establishes: Underwood separately identifies himself as recording a later infrared target.
sourceRecords.doesNotEstablish: Same object independently matched across sorties or all claimed extraordinary manoeuvres.

sourceRecords.locator: NASA UAP FAQ questions 4, 5 and 7 (data requirements and explicit non-adjudication of earlier UAP cases)
sourceRecords.establishes: Scientific need for adequate observational data and calibrated measurements; NASA's report did not review earlier incidents individually.
sourceRecords.doesNotEstablish: A resolution, disproof, proof, independent eyewitness account, or verified sensor reconstruction of the Nimitz incident.

sourceRecords.locator: Mick West, 17 September 2019 opening analysis; FLIR1 tracking/zoom explanation
sourceRecords.establishes: A testable competing interpretation for apparent motion in the separate FLIR1 sequence.
sourceRecords.doesNotEstablish: A conclusive refutation or explanation of all named visual witnesses and original ship radar claims.

sourceRecords.locator: 2019 Entropy paper, section 2.4 Nimitz Encounters and 2.4.1 Kevin Day (RADAR)
sourceRecords.establishes: Knuth, Powell and Reali document radar-operator Kevin Day's later account and estimate motion from reported timings, ranges and flight paths; their derivation openly relies on recalled sensor values.
sourceRecords.doesNotEstablish: Original radar plots, calibrated independent sensor measurements, instrument-derived physical acceleration, a separate independently confirmed incident, or an extraterrestrial explanation.

sourceRecords.locator: U.S. Navy UAP Questions and Answers, Q2 (November 2004 USS Nimitz video circulation)
sourceRecords.establishes: Indexed official Navy public-affairs briefing describes the 2004 video as widely distributed on the ship and its later online publication history.
sourceRecords.doesNotEstablish: First-generation infrared sensor metadata, an uninterrupted video of Fravor's original sighting, independently validated radar acceleration, or nonhuman technology.

reviewTasks: Independent human editor verifies the original government transcript and written witness statement word for word against claim wording.
Second reviewer checks the separately published Dietrich interview and whether each quoted aircrew person is truly independent, without treating repeated reporting as new corroboration.

Seek contemporaneous ship radar log files, aircraft mission records, first-generation FLIR1 and EXIF/telemetry/calibration and documented custody; mark unavailable material as unavailable, not proof of nonexistence.
Obtain independently reproducible motion estimates with target range/time uncertainty bounds and camera-state corrections.
Document what a camera-tracking explanation does and does not explain, separately from initial aircrew visual observations.
Reviewer records conflict-of-interest declaration, any contested findings, signed date and publication approval through an authorised process.

Editorial calibration: separate visual observation, radar testimony, later official FLIR footage, quantitative motion and origin into distinct claim scopes; assign no points to a blended case-level question.

Source-lineage audit: check original Kevin Day accounts and Navy FOIA briefing provenance. Count distinct reported shipboard sensors accurately without treating repeated interviews, a journal modelling paper or official video release as original radar tracks.

withdrawnFirstPass.withdrawnReason: Bundled whether a documented visual observation was reported, distinct shipboard radar reports, official later FLIR footage, precise extraordinary acceleration and object origin into one score. Misleadingly weighted public raw-data accessibility against firsthand and official recording evidence; unjustified as a single case strength percentage.
withdrawnFirstPass.prohibitedUse: Do not display as current score, probability, editorial conclusion or community vote target

evidenceUnits.question: Were visual observations of an unidentified object reported by distinct named aircrew on the same sortie?
evidenceUnits.finding: Two named direct pilot accounts are separately attributable and deserve substantial weight for an observed, not-yet-identified encounter.
evidenceUnits.limits: A genuine report of an unidentified object is not by itself a validated physical performance estimate or proof of an exotic origin.

evidenceUnits.question: What reported tracking was observed by shipboard/airborne radar teams?
evidenceUnits.finding: Fravor testified that Princeton, Nimitz and E-2 systems tracked the target(s); later Kevin Day interviews were used in a peer-reviewed trajectory study. This is credible source material that must not be silently discarded.
evidenceUnits.limits: Accounts of radar detections are not the same as independent access to the original raw returns, sensor calibration or synchronized time/target identification.

evidenceUnits.question: What does the officially released infrared video establish?
evidenceUnits.finding: A real Navy infrared recording from November 2004 was officially released and its history discussed in Navy public-affairs materials.
evidenceUnits.limits: Filmed by a later crew; identity with the earlier sighting and range/acceleration claims cannot be assumed from the official release alone.

evidenceUnits.question: Do the reviewed records verify the claimed speed, rapid acceleration or the alleged sixty-mile displacement?
evidenceUnits.finding: Specific flight-dynamics claims are reported and modelled under assumptions; multiple competing interpretations deserve independent investigation.
evidenceUnits.limits: No original complete synchronized radar or FLIR range/geometry record was independently checked; conditional model outputs are not new physical measurements.

evidenceUnits.question: Do the materials identify nonhuman or extraterrestrial origin?
evidenceUnits.finding: The sources reviewed do not identify an origin.
evidenceUnits.limits: Unidentified does not imply nonhuman or extraterrestrial, and an absent conclusive explanation does not yield a numerical probability for a specific origin.
